c.tagline: All-inclusive beaches on the Caribbean coast

taxi.fareNote: no meters; government-set fixed zone rates, confirm first

emergency.note: 911 works nationwide; tourist police (CESTUR) patrol resort zones and English-speaking help is common in tourist areas.

hood_landmark.Bavaro: Playa Bávaro's long white-sand, palm-lined resort beach
hood_landmark.Cap Cana: Juanillo Beach and the upscale Cap Cana megayacht marina
hood_landmark.Punta Cana Village: Galerías Punta Cana shopping-and-dining plaza near the airport
hood_landmark.Uvero Alto: Secluded Uvero Alto Beach backed by all-inclusive resorts

avoid.reason: Stay within the resort corridor at night; avoid isolated stretches of beach and inland worker towns such as Verón after dark.
Watch for pushy excursion and timeshare touts, motoconcho/taxi overcharging, and petty theft on public beach areas like El Cortecito.

hood_desc: The main resort strip of Punta Cana, with long white-sand beaches lined by all-inclusive resorts, shops and nightlife; suits first-time visitors and beach vacationers wanting the classic resort experience.
An exclusive gated luxury enclave with a marina, golf courses, upscale resorts and villas; suits affluent travelers and honeymooners seeking privacy and high-end amenities.
A leafy residential community near the airport with the Blue Mall, restaurants and boutique hotels, popular with locals and expats; suits travelers wanting a calmer, more authentic non-resort base.
A quieter, secluded stretch of coast north of Bavaro with newer luxury resorts and undeveloped beaches; suits couples and those seeking tranquility away from the crowds.
lodging: Hotel Casa Don Luis Cap Cana by Faranda Boutique
Four Points by Sheraton Puntacana Village

water.note: Avoid tap water; use bottled or purified water, even for brushing teeth.

transit.pay: There is no transit card; pay cash in Dominican pesos on guaguas (RD$35-60, ~$0.60-1) or negotiate taxi fares in cash (USD often accepted). Resort shuttles are usually prepaid or included with excursions, and Uber has limited, inconsistent availability in the Punta Cana/Bávaro area.
transit.hours: Guaguas run roughly 6am-9pm on main roads with no fixed schedule; taxis and resort transfers are available around the clock.
transit.note: Most tourists rely on taxis, resort shuttles or rental cars rather than public buses; guaguas are used mainly by locals on set routes like the Bávaro-Higüey highway.

food.name: La bandera dominicana
food.desc: The national lunch plate: white rice, stewed red beans and meat, usually with salad and fried sweet plantain. Eaten at midday all over the country.

places.name: La Casita de Yeya
places.note: Home-style Dominican kitchen near the airport, celebrated for traditional everyday cooking.

places.name: El Fogon
places.note: Popular Dominican restaurant with the full range of criollo plates at 10 to 20 USD.

places.name: Comedores of Veron
places.note: Roadside canteens where resort staff eat; the cheapest and most authentic bandera in the area.

food.name: Mofongo
food.desc: Green plantains fried then mashed in a wooden pilon with garlic, oil and pork cracklings, often crowned with shrimp, lobster or creole sauce.

places.name: Delicias de Bavaro
places.note: Mofongo specialist reportedly offering up to 28 versions; a local favourite, not a resort menu.

places.name: El Fogon
places.note: Dependable mofongo with chicharron alongside sancocho and other Dominican staples.

places.name: La Casita de Yeya
places.note: Home-cooked mofongo served the way Dominican families make it, garlicky and dense.

food.name: Sancocho
food.desc: Slow-simmered stew of up to seven meats with yuca, yam, green plantain and corn in a garlic, cilantro and oregano broth. Sunday and celebration food.

places.name: La Casita de Yeya
places.note: Best known locally for its sancocho; the reason Dominicans drive out here for lunch.

places.name: El Fogon
places.note: Sancocho on the regular menu rather than only at weekends, with chicharron on the side.

places.name: Comedores of Veron
places.note: Neighbourhood canteens often cook a sancocho pot on weekends; ask what is on that day.

food.name: Pescado frito con tostones
food.desc: Whole reef fish fried crisp and served with twice-fried green plantain discs, salad and a squeeze of lime. Beach-shack cooking at its best.

places.name: Captain Cook
places.note: Beachfront seafood institution where you pick the catch from ice before it hits the grill.

places.name: El Cortecito beach comedores
places.note: Row of simple local shacks on the public beach frying the day's catch to order.

places.name: Playa Blanca
places.note: Smarter beach club version of fried fish and tostones, with loungers and calm water.

food.name: Chicharron and pica pollo
food.desc: Deep-fried pork belly chunks and crackly Dominican fried chicken, sold by weight with tostones and hot sauce. Standard roadside and late-night food.

places.name: El Fogon
places.note: Chicharron done properly, crisp outside and juicy inside, alongside the criollo mains.

places.name: Friusa pica pollo stands
places.note: The local barrio where Dominicans queue for fried chicken; busiest on weekend nights.

places.name: Comedores of Veron
places.note: Roadside chicharroneras sell pork by the pound; point at what looks freshest.

food.name: Mangu
food.desc: Mashed boiled green plantain topped with pickled red onion, served for breakfast with fried cheese, salami and egg as los tres golpes.

places.name: La Casita de Yeya
places.note: Classic Dominican breakfast served the traditional way with los tres golpes.

places.name: Delicias de Bavaro
places.note: Plantain specialists, so mangu is a natural fit alongside the mofongo list.

places.name: El Cortecito comedores
places.note: Small local breakfast counters serving mangu long before the resort buffets open.

food.name: Mamajuana
food.desc: Rum, red wine and honey steeped over a jar of tree bark, roots and herbs. Sweet, earthy and famously credited with all sorts of powers.

places.name: Huracan Cafe
places.note: Beachfront bar and restaurant pouring mamajuana with an ocean view; popular at sunset.

places.name: El Fogon
places.note: House-steeped mamajuana served after dinner rather than the sweeter bottled version.

places.name: Bibijagua Market
places.note: Local craft market where vendors sell jars and bottles to take home; taste before buying.

food.name: Morir sonando and chinola juice
food.desc: Morir sonando blends orange juice with milk, sugar and ice; chinola is passion fruit, squeezed fresh and served at every Dominican breakfast table.

places.name: El Cortecito juice stands
places.note: Beachside juice bars blending chinola, lechosa and morir sonando to order.

places.name: Huracan Cafe
places.note: Tropical juices and batidas served all day on the sand, alcoholic versions available.

places.name: Delicias de Bavaro
places.note: Fresh natural juices poured with the Dominican mains at local prices.

landmarks: Bávaro Beach
A long stretch of powder-white sand and turquoise Caribbean water widely rated one of the best beaches in the world, ideal for classic tropical postcard shots.
Hoyo Azul (Scape Park)
A strikingly blue natural cenote pool set inside a limestone cave surrounded by jungle, one of the region's most photographed natural wonders.
Basílica Nuestra Señora de la Altagracia
A soaring modernist cathedral in nearby Higüey and the country's most important pilgrimage site, notable for its bold parabolic-arch design.
Cap Cana Marina
An upscale marina lined with yachts, cliffside pools, and dramatic coastline, a favorite for luxury lifestyle and sunset photography.
Cabeza de Toro Beach
A quieter cove beach with calm lagoon-like waters and mangrove channels, great for tranquil waterfront shots away from crowds.
Punta Cana Coast
The namesake easternmost point of the Dominican Republic, where the Caribbean Sea and Atlantic Ocean converge along miles of resort-lined shoreline.
Indigenous Eyes Ecological Park (Reserva Ecológica Ojos Indígenas)
Twelve spring-fed freshwater lagoons threaded through coastal forest inside Puntacana Resort, with trails, an iguana farm, and swimming holes named for the Taíno people.
Manatí Park
A Bávaro theme park of orchid-filled gardens, native wildlife exhibits, and dolphin and sea lion shows built around Dominican flora and fauna.
Marinarium
A reef preserve off Cabeza de Toro reached by boat, where visitors wade among nurse sharks and southern stingrays in shallow open water.
Coco Bongo Punta Cana
A cavernous Los Corales nightclub staging acrobatic circus-style shows, live bands, and open-bar parties that run from midnight past dawn.

train.note: The Dominican Republic has no intercity passenger railway (only the Santo Domingo metro). Travel is by bus or car.

bus.note: There are no international buses from Punta Cana itself - cross-border coaches to Haiti (Caribe Tours, Capital Coach Line) leave from Santo Domingo, about 3h away. Local operators such as Expreso Bavaro link Punta Cana with Santo Domingo. A passport is required for Haiti.

intl.to: San Juan, Puerto Rico (departs Santo Domingo)

ferry.note: No ferries run from Punta Cana. Ferries del Caribe sails overnight from Santo Domingo (about 3-4h away by road) to San Juan, Puerto Rico several days a week. Bring your passport.

half.name: Saona Island
half.blurb: A protected palm-fringed island of white sand and natural pools reached by catamaran or speedboat.

half.name: Altos de Chavón
half.blurb: A recreated Mediterranean village of stone above the Chavón River, with an amphitheater and galleries.

half.name: Isla Catalina
half.blurb: A tiny uninhabited island ringed by coral reefs, prized for snorkeling and diving.

half.name: Los Haitises National Park
half.blurb: Mangrove channels, limestone karst islets and caves with ancient Taíno rock art await explorers.

half.name: Macao Beach
half.blurb: A wild, undeveloped stretch of golden sand and rolling surf popular with beginner surfers.

full.name: Santo Domingo
full.blurb: The Americas' oldest colonial city, its Zona Colonial packed with cobbled streets and history.
